newsitem.title: USA: US senators urge White House to adjust budget base.
newsitem.headline: US senators urge White House to adjust budget base.

text.p: Senior Republican and Democratic senators urged the Clinton administration on Sunday to update the government's cost of living index to avoid stalling next year's budget debate.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has said the Consumer Price Index (CPI) needs to be changed to reflect the nation's economy more accurately, but said the technical adjustments could not be made in time for the fiscal 1998 budget plan.
"Hopefully, they'll reconsider that signal," Sen. Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican, said on NBC television's "Meet the Press."

Government programmes, including Social Security payments, are tied to inflation increases. According to the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York, the government could save $1 trillion in 10 years by adjusting the consumer price index.
Speaking on the same show, Moynihan said unless the administration changed the cost of living calculations, "then we won't have a current budget process of any consequence."

"This is an area where you will see Congress not willing to move forward unless we have a signal from the administration that they're going to be willing to use an accurate CPI," said Nickles, who is Senate Republican whip.

The Senate Finance Committee is due to release Wednesday a final report on the CPI by a bipartisan commission headed by Stanford economist Michael Boskin. In a preliminary report, the commission said the CPI overstated inflation by between 0.7 and 2 percent.

Looking ahead at the agenda for the new Congress, Nickles and Moynihan said problems with the Medicare programme for the elderly had to be addressed, but Moynihan predicted Congress would do "nothing (on Medicare), unless we have some money."
Nickles said the Republicans would work with President Bill Clinton if he offered a proposal to save the programme from going broke.

Congress should not postpone action by setting up a commission to find ways to fund the programme, as suggested by some Republicans and Democrats, he said. "I think putting it off to a bipartisan commission to solve the problem a year from now is ridiculous," Nickles said.

Both senators said they did not expect the new Congress to make any major changes in the landmark welfare law passed this year and said states should be given time to try to move people off welfare into jobs before Congress reviews the law.

Moynihan, a vocal critic of the law that ended the 61-year-old federal guarantee of assistance to the poor, said he welcomed first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton's plans to monitor the impact of the changes.

But Nickles questioned whether she would conduct an impartial review. "To have her be the overseer for the administration if she's philosophically opposed to the bill, to the big changes we made, I think it would be the wrong person to be in charge of the review," he said.
